units.text: To create a patch that changes an older version of a package into a newer version, first make a copy of the older and newer versions in adjacent subdirectories. It is common to do that by unpacking ⟦0⟧ archives of the two versions.
units.sourceHTML: To create a patch that changes an older version of a package into a newer version, first make a copy of the older and newer versions in adjacent subdirectories. It is common to do that by unpacking tar archives of the two versions.

units.text: To generate the patch, use the command ‘⟦0⟧’ where ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ identify the old and new directories. The names ⟦3⟧ and ⟦4⟧ should not contain any slashes. The ⟦5⟧ option lets the patch create and remove files; ⟦6⟧ lets the patch update non-text files; ⟦7⟧ generates useful timestamps and enough context; and ⟦8⟧ lets the patch update subdirectories. units.sourceHTML: To generate the patch, use the command ‘diff -Naur old new’ where old and new identify the old and new directories. The names old and new should not contain any slashes. The -N option lets the patch create and remove files; -a lets the patch update non-text files; -u generates useful timestamps and enough context; and -r lets the patch update subdirectories. units.text: Tell your recipients how to apply the patches. This should include which working directory to use, and which ⟦0⟧ options to use; the option ‘⟦1⟧’ is recommended. Test your procedure by pretending to be a recipient and applying your patches to a copy of the original files.
units.sourceHTML: Tell your recipients how to apply the patches. This should include which working directory to use, and which patch options to use; the option ‘-p1’ is recommended. Test your procedure by pretending to be a recipient and applying your patches to a copy of the original files.
